In Belo Horizonte, the EVITA long-term trial involving over 5,700 schoolchildren showed dengue and chikungunya infections fell by about 68-69% in areas released with Wolbachia mosquitoes compared with control areas. - Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti released in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, substantially reduced arboviral infections among schoolchildren in the EVITA trial (2020–2024). Nearly 6,000 children were randomized to Wolbachia deployment or standard control measures; routine blood tests showed arboviral infection positivity of 4% in Wolbachia areas versus 14% in control areas, during the city’s largest dengue outbreak in its history. The intervention was 68.5% effective against dengue and 73.3% against chikungunya. Wolbachia bacteria inhibit virus replication in mosquitoes and spread through offspring, enabling local transmission suppression. The four-year study provides strong evidence that large-scale Wolbachia releases can reduce dengue and chikungunya transmissions in dense urban settings.

articleSummary: Porcine immune systems can generate monoclonal antibodies recognizing conserved influenza A structures and adaptive mutations across subtypes, per Pirbright Institute. articleHeadline: The Black Death Won't End in an Instant: Here's What Happens Next
articleSummary: Second Plague Pandemic continues after the Black Death, with a new PNAS study from the University of Tartu detailing repeated plague resurgence across Western Eurasia through the 14th–18th centuries. Using refined phylochronology that fuses radiocarbon dating, genetic timelines, historical records, and 26 Yersinia pestis genomes from 11 archaeological sites in Estonia, Russia, England, the Netherlands, and Switzerland, researchers dated 75 genomes with improved accuracy. The work links multiple plague waves to city- or region-specific outbreaks and identifies substantial diversification of Y. pestis lineages around 1450–1500, suggesting new rodent reservoirs in urban and rural settings. A proposed connection to the Great Renaissance Drought is discussed, potentially driving rodent die-offs or migrations toward humans and accelerating transmission. The findings show repeated introduction of plague into Estonia starting in the late 14th century, highlighting the enduring historical and global health relevance of the disease.

articleHeadline: Seven days on ECMO save a young man with dengue fever and heart complications.
articleSummary: A 24-year-old man developed dengue fever that progressed to cardiogenic shock with acute myocarditis. Public health measures include drinking plenty of clean water, maintaining environmental hygiene, eliminating mosquito breeding sites, and ensuring children receive routine vaccinations. Calls for stronger logistical support for frontline surveillance—motorbikes, vehicles, and fuel—to enable rapid investigations in remote communities and strengthen community-level surveillance.
